cards.back: The formal written offer to sell securities required by Section 10 of the Securities Act of 1933. It discloses material information about the issuer and the offering and must be delivered to investors in registered public offerings.

An investor who meets income (>$200K individual / $300K joint for two prior years) or net worth (>$1M excluding primary residence) tests, certain institutions, or qualifies via professional credentials (Series 7, 65, or 82). Eligible to purchase securities in private placements under Regulation D.

An offering method in which the underwriter purchases the entire issue from the issuer and resells it to the public, assuming the risk of any unsold shares. Contrasted with best efforts, where the underwriter acts only as an agent.

An SEC registration allowing an issuer to register securities for sale over a period of up to three years (or longer for WKSIs) and offer them in tranches as market conditions warrant, without filing a new registration each time.

A negotiable receipt issued by a U.S. bank representing shares of a foreign company held on deposit abroad. ADRs trade in U.S. markets in U.S. dollars and facilitate domestic investment in foreign equities; holders bear currency risk and generally lack voting rights.
Preferred stock that requires all skipped (omitted) dividends to be paid in full before any common stock dividend may be declared. Provides greater dividend protection than straight preferred.

A long-term equity security giving the holder the right (not the obligation) to buy the issuer's stock at a fixed price, typically issued at exercise prices above current market and often attached as a sweetener to bond or preferred stock offerings.

SEC rule governing the resale of restricted and control securities. Imposes a holding period (6 months for reporting issuers), volume limits, manner-of-sale, current-information requirements, and electronic Form 144 filing on EDGAR for affiliates.

A municipal bond backed by the full faith, credit, and taxing power of the issuer. Repayment relies on the issuer's ability to levy taxes (typically ad valorem property taxes at the local level), and issuance often requires voter approval.

A municipal bond payable solely from revenues generated by a specific project or facility (e.g., toll road, airport). Not backed by taxing power; analyzed primarily by the debt service coverage ratio.

The total annualized return a bondholder earns if the bond is held to maturity, accounting for coupon income plus any gain or loss from purchase price relative to par. Reflects the bond's internal rate of return.

A short-term, negotiable money market instrument used to finance international trade. It is a time draft drawn on and accepted by a bank, which guarantees payment at maturity (typically 270 days or less).

The per-share value of a mutual fund or other investment company, calculated as (total fund assets − total fund liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding. Open-end fund orders are executed at the next computed NAV (forward pricing).

A discounted sales charge level on Class A mutual fund shares triggered when an investor's purchase reaches specified dollar thresholds. Investors may aggregate purchases via a Letter of Intent or Rights of Accumulation to qualify.

An investment company classification under the Investment Company Act of 1940 that issues redeemable units representing an undivided interest in a fixed, unmanaged portfolio of securities, with a stated termination date.

An annual fee deducted from a mutual fund's assets to cover distribution and shareholder servicing expenses, authorized under SEC Rule 12b-1 of the Investment Company Act of 1940. Disclosed in the prospectus and capped under FINRA Rule 2341.

A municipal fund security established under IRC Section 529 that provides tax-deferred growth and tax-free qualified distributions for education expenses. Includes prepaid tuition and savings plan variants; SECURE 2.0 permits limited rollovers to a Roth IRA.
A pooled, generally illiquid investment (typically a limited partnership) that passes through income, gains, losses, deductions, and credits directly to investors, avoiding entity-level taxation.

A Real Estate Investment Trust — a pooled investment vehicle that invests in real estate equity, mortgages, or both. To avoid corporate taxation, a REIT must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders; distributions are taxed as ordinary income.

A private, generally unregistered pooled investment vehicle (typically a limited partnership) sold to accredited or qualified investors. Characterized by high minimums, performance fees, leverage, limited liquidity, and broad investment latitude.
An options strategy in which the writer of a call option simultaneously owns the underlying stock. The strategy generates premium income and is considered the least risky option-writing position.

A custodial account established under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. Assets are irrevocable gifts owned by the minor but managed by a custodian until the minor reaches the age of majority defined by state law.

An account in which the customer has granted prior written authorization permitting the registered representative to choose security, action, or amount without contacting the customer for each trade. All discretionary orders must be marked as such and reviewed promptly by a principal.

The minimum amount that must be withdrawn annually from a traditional IRA or qualified plan beginning at age 73 (under SECURE 2.0). Failure to take the RMD triggers a 25% excise tax on the shortfall (10% if timely corrected).
The risk inherent in the overall market that cannot be eliminated through diversification. Includes market risk, interest rate risk, inflation (purchasing power) risk, and currency risk.

The risk that interest or principal cash flows from a fixed-income investment will have to be reinvested at a lower prevailing rate, reducing total return. Zero-coupon bonds eliminate this risk over their term.
A risk-mitigation strategy that spreads investments across different securities, sectors, asset classes, or geographies to reduce nonsystematic (issuer-specific) risk within a portfolio.

A dividend taxed at the long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20%) rather than at ordinary income rates. Requires holding the underlying common stock more than 60 days during the 121-day period surrounding the ex-dividend date.

An IRS rule that disallows a capital loss deduction if the taxpayer purchases a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the loss sale. The disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of the replacement security.
The taxable yield that would equal the after-tax yield of a tax-exempt municipal bond, calculated as municipal yield ÷ (1 − investor's marginal tax bracket). Used to compare munis to taxable bonds.
The interest rate the Federal Reserve charges member banks for short-term loans through the discount window. Lowering it eases credit; raising it tightens credit.

The interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserve balances. Targeted by the FOMC as a primary tool of monetary policy and influenced through open market operations and interest on reserve balances (IORB).

An economic statistic that tends to change before the broader economy does, used to forecast future activity. Examples include the S&P 500, building permits, average weekly manufacturing hours, and the M2 money supply.

Securities Investor Protection Corporation — a nonprofit membership corporation created by the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 that protects customers of failed broker-dealers up to $500,000 per separate-capacity customer, including a $250,000 limit on cash.

Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board — the SRO that writes rules governing broker-dealers and municipal advisors in the municipal securities market. The MSRB does not enforce its own rules; enforcement falls to FINRA, the SEC, and bank regulators.
A FinCEN report (Form 112) that a financial institution must file for cash transactions exceeding $10,000 in a single day by or on behalf of one person, whether in one transaction or aggregated.

A confidential report filed with FinCEN within 30 calendar days of detecting suspicious activity (extendable to 60 days if no suspect is identified). Required for transactions of $5,000 or more involving suspected illegal activity; disclosure to the subject is prohibited.

Trading securities on the basis of material, nonpublic information in breach of a fiduciary duty or other relationship of trust. Prohibited under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; ITSFEA permits civil penalties up to three times the profit gained or loss avoided.

The Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer — filed by a member firm through FINRA's CRD system to register an associated person. Disclosure events must generally be amended within 30 days (10 business days for statutory disqualification events).

The Uniform Termination Notice for Securities Industry Registration — filed by a member firm in CRD within 30 days of an associated person's termination, with a copy provided to the former associated person within the same period.
Any business activity by a registered person outside the scope of the relationship with the member firm. Requires prior written notice to the firm before engaging in the activity.
